ce:section.ce:para: The ductile-to-brittle transition (DBT) is a critical phenomenon in materials science, characterized by an abrupt shift in failure mode over a narrow temperature range. This transition is a defining characteristic of body-centered cubic (BCC) metals and frequently precipitates catastrophic structural failure [1–3]. Tungsten is chosen as the prototype material both for its engineering relevance and its fundamental significance. Its high ductile-to-brittle transition temperature (DBTT, 500–900 K) severely limits its use in nuclear fusion environments [4–6]. Moreover, the extensive thermomechanical processing applied to tungsten to reduce brittleness generates strongly anisotropic, elongated grain structures. This non‑equiaxed microstructure offers an ideal testbed for investigating how grain morphology—a factor absent from conventional models—affects the DBTT. For decades, the field has relied on empirical Hall‑Petch‑type linear relations that link DBTT solely to grain size [7–9]. Although such correlations capture the trend of decreasing DBTT with grain refinement, they lack a mechanistic foundation, as yielding and brittle fracture involve fundamentally distinct processes. This limitation has motivated the development of physics‑based models aimed at closing this critical gap [10–12].

Recent mechanistic insights reveal that the DBT in BCC metals is governed by the disparate mobilities of screw and edge dislocations and their collective influence on dislocation multiplication [13]. The non-planar core structure of a/2<111> screw dislocations in the BCC lattice renders their motion highly dependent on thermal activation, leading to a pronounced velocity difference between screw and edge segments. At low temperatures, this disparity impedes the efficiency of dislocation multiplication, leading to a deficit of mobile dislocations required to accommodate plastic strain, which ultimately triggers brittle fracture [14–16]. In direct support of this model, in-situ observations in various BCC metals have confirmed a distinct difference in dislocation bowing-out curvature at the source between the ductile (high-temperature) and brittle (low-temperature) regimes [17]. Subsequent work has established a unified model that quantitatively links dislocation source efficiency to DBT behavior, showing that brittleness can be mitigated by enhancing either the efficiency or the density of dislocation sources [18].

Electron backscatter diffraction (EBSD) was used to characterize the five tungsten materials investigated in this study: rotary swaged W (RS-W), bidirectionally rolled W (BR-W), unidirectionally rolled W (UR-W), fine-grained potassium-doped W (FG-WK), and ultrafine-grained potassium-doped W (UFG-WK). To ensure the universal applicability and industrial recognition of the results, all samples were derived from standard commercial-grade products. The RS-W was a commercial high-purity (99.99 %) sintered and rotary-swaged tungsten bar purchased from China New Metal Material Technology Co., Ltd. The BR-W and UR-W samples were subsequently fabricated by bidirectionally and unidirectionally rolling the RS-W material, respectively, to a total deformation of 30 % at 1300 °C. The FG-WK and UFG-WK samples were commercial potassium-doped tungsten rolled plates (containing ∼80 ppm K) purchased from AT&M Technology Co., Ltd. Three-dimensional (3D) grain sizes for all samples were quantified from EBSD-generated inverse pole figure maps using Nano Measurer software. In potassium-doped tungsten, potassium is known to exist as gaseous dispersoids at grain boundaries during high-temperature processing, which effectively refines the grain structure. However, existing experimental and theoretical analyses indicate that trace potassium doping does not influence the DBTT at the low-to-intermediate temperatures relevant to this study [19,20]. Therefore, the inclusion of K-doped tungsten is justified and serves to validate the current model against a broader range of grain sizes and microstructures.

The DBTT of each sample was systematically determined using small punch testing. This technique is particularly effective for the precise identification of the DBTT across broad temperature ranges under controlled, low-strain-rate conditions, providing robust data for model validation [21]. Square plate specimens (6 mm × 6 mm × 0.45 mm) were prepared for testing. To maximize the activation of grain boundary dislocation sources, which are prevalent on the normal direction (ND) planes in rolled tungsten, specimens were loaded precisely along the ND. All specimens were prepared to meet stringent surface requirements. They were first mechanically ground and polished to achieve micrometer-level flatness, followed by electrochemical polishing for 10 min at 273 K under a constant potential of 15 V in a 0.45 wt % NaOH aqueous solution. Prior to testing, both specimens and fixtures were thermally equilibrated at the target temperature for at least one hour. The tests were performed under displacement control at a crosshead speed of 0.2 mm/min and were terminated after a 20 % load drop from the maximum value.

The efficiency of dislocation multiplication at a source is dictated by the mobility disparity between its screw and edge components [13]. At low temperatures, the motion of screw dislocations in BCC metals is governed by the thermally activated process of kink-pair nucleation and migration, rendering them significantly less mobile than edge dislocations. As the temperature rises, the rate-limiting mechanism for screw dislocations transitions to phonon-drag, the same mechanism that governs edge dislocation motion, allowing their mobility to increase substantially [23–25]. Using this framework and experimentally measured values of the critical resolved shear stress for single-crystal tungsten [28], the temperature-dependent velocities of screw and edge dislocations, and the resulting source multiplication efficiency (

As illustrated schematically in Fig. 1(a), an expanding dislocation loop becomes highly anisotropic: the edge segments bow out rapidly while the screw segments remain nearly immobile. This pinning effect hinders the lateral expansion and cycling of the dislocation source, leading to low multiplication efficiency and promoting brittle fracture.

With increasing temperature, the thermally activated motion of screw dislocations accelerates, while the mobility of edge dislocations gradually decreases due to increased phonon scattering. This convergence of velocities enables a more cooperative motion of the entire dislocation line, facilitating the cycling of the source and dramatically increasing the rate of dislocation multiplication. This transition from inefficient to efficient source operation corresponds to the material's transition from brittle to ductile. Previous work has established that a critical efficiency of α = 0.5 marks the onset of efficient dislocation multiplication in tungsten [13]. By correlating this critical efficiency to the DBTT, the model calculates a transition temperature of 685 K. This value is in excellent agreement with the experimentally determined DBTT for high-purity recrystallized tungsten [18].

Fig. 2 (a–e) presents the 3D inverse pole figure maps for the five tungsten materials: RS-W, BR-W, UR-W, FG-WK, and UFG-WK. The maps reveal a clear trend of grain refinement and strengthening of crystallographic texture with increasing degrees of plastic deformation during processing. Quantitative analysis of the grain size distributions provided the average value and standard deviation along three orthogonal directions for each material.

Based on the mechanical processing history, grain size, and grain shape of each sample, we estimated the order of magnitude of the total dislocation density, the fraction of mobile dislocations, and the resulting pre-existing mobile dislocation density (
ρ i
), as summarized in Table S2. In this framework,
ρ i
is estimated based on the physically grounded evolution of dislocation character and network configuration with thermomechanical processing history. For BCC tungsten, the high lattice friction associated with screw dislocations results in significantly lower mobility compared to edge and mixed dislocations in the temperature regime relevant to the DBTT. Accordingly, the fraction of non-screw dislocations provides a physically meaningful approximation of the mobile dislocation fraction. Previous quantitative TEM analyses [22] have demonstrated that increasing deformation severity and processing temperature promote intensified dislocation interactions and a systematic transition toward dislocation networks increasingly dominated by non-screw segments. Based on this established microstructural evolution, mobile dislocation fractions of ∼50 %, ∼60 %, ∼70 %, and ∼80 % were assigned to represent the characteristic configurations of recrystallized, lightly deformed/annealed, cold-worked, and hot-worked states, respectively. These assigned values reflect a physically reasoned scaling of dislocation activity with processing history and are consistent with reported ranges of mobile (or non-screw) dislocation densities in the literature for BCC metals under comparable conditions [29,33–35]. Furthermore, sensitivity analyses confirm that the predicted DBTT trends and their dependence on grain size are robust against moderate variations in the assumed mobile dislocation fraction, underscoring that the model’s conclusions do not rely on the precise tuning of this parameter.

The DBT in the five tungsten materials was characterized by small punch tests, with the normalized small punch energy (
E n
) plotted as a function of temperature in Fig. 3 (a–e). Each
E n
value was obtained by integrating the corresponding load-displacement curve (Fig. S1) and normalizing by the peak load. The behavior of the RS-W sample is illustrative: in the 623–723 K range, the material fails instantaneously at a low load, with only a slight increase in
E n
, which is characteristic of brittle fracture. As the temperature rises to 773–798 K, both the peak load and
E n
increase significantly, but failure remains abrupt, indicating a semi-brittle transition state. Above 823 K, the load-displacement curves show a gradual decay after the peak load, demonstrating significant crack growth resistance, and the
E n
values plateau, confirming a fully ductile response. The DBTT for each of the five materials was determined by fitting the data using Eq. (1) and is indicated in Fig. 3(a–e).

Fractographic analysis confirmed the DBTT determined from the mechanical tests (Fig. 3(f–t)). In the brittle regime, the fracture surfaces are dominated by intergranular and cleavage facets, with no evidence of significant dislocation activity near the crack path. In the semi-brittle transition region, numerous slip bands and deformed grains appear near the crack, indicating that activated dislocations accommodated limited plastic deformation; however, cleavage remains the dominant failure mechanism, suggesting that dislocation activity was insufficient to blunt the crack tip. In the fully ductile regime, the fracture surfaces exhibit a delaminated, deformed structure, confirming widespread dislocation activation. The macroscopic fracture morphology (insets, Fig. 3(f–t)) also clearly distinguishes the failure modes, with the crack path systematically transitioning from linear (brittle) to circumferential (ductile) as temperature increases.

Notably, the UFG-WK material exhibited localized circumferential cracking even at lower temperatures, and its peak load and
E n
values were significantly higher than those of other materials displaying a similar brittle fracture mode. This finding is consistent with previous observations in BCC chromium [36]. These results provide direct evidence that a high density of pre-existing mobile dislocations, introduced during severe plastic deformation, can promote limited plasticity even at low temperatures where dislocation sources are largely inactive. This confirms the intimate link between the DBT and the pre-existing mobile dislocation density. Although minor surface oxidation was observed in some high-temperature tests, while the load-displacement curves are not affected, indicating that it does not affect the deformation and failure mode.

To rigorously test the current model and re-evaluate the empirical Hall-Petch-type relationship between DBTT and grain size, we compiled a comprehensive dataset. This dataset includes the five tungsten materials from this study and an additional twenty-four sets of experimental data reported in the literature [22,37–43]. The literature data were obtained using various standard methods for DBTT determination, including single-edge notched tensile (SENT) tests, Charpy impact tests (CIT), and small punch tests (SPT). To account for systematic differences arising from test methodology (e.g., strain rate, stress state, and specimen thickness), error bars are incorporated to represent the intrinsic DBTT range for each material. According to the widely cited empirical relation, DBTT is expected to decrease linearly with the inverse square root of the grain size (typically the average grain size in the normal direction, d ND in µm−1/2) [38]. As shown in Fig. 4 (a), while this linear relationship captures the general trend of decreasing DBTT with grain refinement, the significant data scatter precludes a precise quantitative description with a single slope and intercept. Detailed parameters for all materials are provided in Tables S3 and S4.

In contrast, when the same dataset is analyzed using the current proposed theoretical model, a fundamentally different relationship emerges. The current model correlates the DBTT with
Σ
r
(in µm−1), the sum of the reciprocals of the 3D average grain sizes. As complete 3D grain size data were not available for all literature materials, missing dimensions were estimated based on processing histories and by comparison with similar materials (Table S3); these points are identified by semi-filled symbols in Fig. 4(a, b) [42,43].

Fig. 4(b) illustrates the predictive method of the current model. The green dashed curve represents the predicted DBTT considering only the contribution from dislocations generated by grain boundaries and Frank-Read sources. The red dashed curve represents the full model, which incorporates the additional effect of the pre-existing mobile dislocation density (
ρ i
​). The calculations show this effect is negligible for materials with low prior deformation, where
ρ i
is low (∼1011–1012 m−2). However, for severely deformed materials with substantially higher
ρ i
(∼1013–1014 m−2), the pre-existing dislocations can reduce the DBTT by as much as 200 K. Evidently, the full model (red curve)—which predicts a nonlinear decrease in DBTT with increasing

​ —captures the experimental trend with much greater fidelity than the traditional linear relationship. This theoretical framework shows excellent agreement with experimental data, enabling quantitative prediction of the DBTT from fundamental microstructural parameters.

This relationship originates from the critical role of grain boundaries, which act as obstacles to dislocation motion. Consequently, grain refinement shortens the mean free path for dislocations, accelerating the accumulation of dislocation density and thereby increasing the yield strength [44–46].

By empirical extension, a Hall-Petch-type relation was assumed to describe the intrinsic connection between the DBTT and grain size in BCC metal [38,47]:

This framework, which has been influential for over half a century, posits that finer grains reduce the spacing between dislocation sources at grain boundaries near a crack tip, allowing more dislocations to be activated and emitted to blunt the crack [48–50]. Notably, the Hall-Petch-type relationship was prescient in identifying the critical role of grain boundary dislocation sources in determining the DBTT. However, the model’s direct adoption of the yield strength formalism represents its fundamental limitation. By construction, it is insensitive to the critical, temperature-dependent dislocation multiplication efficiency—the critical mechanism that governs the transition from ductile-to-brittle behavior—and is therefore incapable of capturing the true nonlinear nature of the DBTT-grain size relationship. This limitation results in the significant deviation observed between experimental data and model predictions (Fig. 4(a)), making it impossible to quantitatively describe the intrinsic DBTT-grain size relationship with fixed values of
T 0
and
k DBT
.

In contrast to the scalar grain size used in the Hall-Petch-type formulation, the current model introduces the grain boundary area-to-volume ratio (
Σ
r
) as a rigorous geometric descriptor. The simplified geometric representation is intentionally chosen to preserve the correct three-dimensional grain-boundary area-to-volume ratio, which is the physically relevant quantity governing dislocation emission, even for highly anisotropic grains. This parameter provides a unified physical interpretation of how both grain size and grain shape govern the DBTT. In thermomechanically processed tungsten, the formation of elongated, pancake-shaped grains results in a significantly higher
Σ
r
compared to equiaxed grains of equivalent volume. Mechanistically, this high specific grain boundary area corresponds to a distinct increase in the spatial density of potential dislocation sources. At low temperatures, where the operation of individual sources is kinetically limited by the sluggish motion of screw dislocations, this enhanced source density becomes critical: it increases the total capacity to generate the sufficient mobile edge dislocation population required to accommodate applied strain, thereby effectively suppressing brittle fracture. Consequently, the nonlinear relationship revealed by the model reflects the fundamental dependence of macroscopic ductility on the three-dimensional spatial availability of dislocation sources. Furthermore, because the current model is built upon a universal theoretical foundation, it holds promise for extension to other BCC metals, such as molybdenum, niobium, and iron. Table S1 provides the key parameters for tungsten, including the Peierls stress (
τ p
) and the pre-exponential factor for the nucleation enthalpy (
Δ
H 0
). These parameters can be adjusted for other specific metallic systems, enabling the quantitative prediction of their DBTTs.

While the current model shows excellent overall agreement with experimental data (Fig. 4(b)), a closer analysis of the deviations is necessary to understand its predictive limitations. Notably, data points for which 3D grain size was estimated (semi-filled symbols) exhibit greater scatter than those with complete experimental data (solid symbols). This highlights the importance of complete 3D microstructural characterization for accurately modeling the spatial distribution of dislocation sources and predicting the DBTT. To rigorously evaluate the model’s reliability, we therefore focused our analysis on the materials for which full 3D data was available.

The DBTT for each material is determined as the temperature at which the calculated mobile dislocation density, evolving with temperature, intersects a critical threshold required for ductile behavior (Fig. 4(c and d)). This threshold was set to
ρ DBT
= 6.50 × 1014 m−2, an experimental value adopted from previous studies on tungsten [22], while the saturation density reflecting the balance between dislocation multiplication and dislocation dynamic recovery was set to ρ = 1.5 × 1015 m−2 [51].

As shown in Fig. 4(c), for the three tungsten materials (FG-WK, UR-W, BR-W) in or near the fine-grained regime (0.075<
Σ
r
< 3.3 µm−1, 450<DBTT<700 K), the deviation between model-predicted and experimentally measured DBTT values is remarkably small, within 15 K. When accounting for microstructural heterogeneity by incorporating one standard deviation in grain size (Fig. 5 (b–d)), the experimental values fall entirely within the predicted range. This confirms the model’s high predictive accuracy in this conventional grain size regime. However, for the UFG-WK in the ultrafine-grained regime (
Σ
r
> 3.3 µm−1, DBTT < 450 K), the experimental DBTT is approximately 8 K below the predicted range even after considering grain size distribution (Fig. 5(a)). Conversely, for the RS-W in the coarse-grained regime (
Σ
r
< 0.075 µm−1, DBTT > 700 K), the measured value exceeds the predicted range by about 80 K (Fig. 5(e)).

This trend is corroborated by the larger literature dataset (Fig. 4). The model’s accuracy is highest for fine-grained materials, where deformation is dominated by the dislocation emission and multiplication mechanisms that form the core of the current model. In contrast, the model systematically overestimates the DBTT of ultrafine-grained materials, with deviations of 25 to 100 K that increase as grain size decreases. For coarse-grained samples, the model systematically underestimates the DBTT, with discrepancies of up to 200 K that become more pronounced as grain size increases.

These systematic deviations likely arise from important non-dislocation-related mechanisms that are not incorporated in the current framework. For ultrafine-grained materials, extrinsic toughening mechanisms become significant. The pronounced pancake-shaped grain morphology resulting from severe plastic deformation can promote crack deflection, and a strong <110>//RD crystallographic texture is widely reported to enhance ductility [52,53]. Both factors would suppress brittle fracture, consistent with the observed lower-than-predicted DBTTs. For coarse-grained materials (RS-W), the model systematically underestimates the DBTT, with discrepancies of up to 200 K that become more pronounced as grain size increases. This specific deviation points to the dominance of extrinsic embrittlement mechanisms—particularly grain boundary impurity segregation—which are not explicitly captured in the current intrinsic dislocation-based framework. Although direct chemical characterization was not performed in this study, it is well established that interstitial impurities (e.g., P, O, C) in tungsten tend to segregate to grain boundaries, significantly reducing cohesive strength [54–57]. This effect is notoriously exacerbated in coarse-grained or recrystallized microstructures, where the reduced total grain boundary area leads to higher local impurity concentrations for a given nominal impurity content. In this scenario, premature intergranular fracture initiates before the critical dislocation density predicted by the model can be generated. Therefore, the model prediction should be interpreted as the ‘intrinsic’ lower bound of the DBTT determined by dislocation dynamics, while the experimentally measured elevation reflects the additional embrittling contribution of impurity segregation. Quantifying these complex, non-dislocation-based mechanisms poses a considerable challenge. Their emergence at extreme grain sizes defines the boundaries where the current purely dislocation-centric framework must be augmented by extrinsic toughening or embrittlement models. The current study thus provides a foundational baseline for isolating and studying these secondary effects.

In summary, a mechanistically grounded theoretical model has been developed that successfully surpasses the long-standing empirical Hall-Petch-type relationship for the DBTT in tungsten. This work shifts the paradigm from simple empirical correlation to a fundamental understanding governed by the efficiency of dislocation multiplication, resolving the intrinsic nonlinear relationship between grain size and DBTT. While this analysis delineates the grain size regimes where dislocation dynamics are dominant, it also provides a physically grounded baseline against which the contributions of secondary, non-dislocation-based mechanisms—such as crystallographic texture or grain boundary embrittlement—can be systematically assessed in future studies. Given its foundation in universal physical principles, the framework established here is not limited to tungsten and is expected to offer a powerful, transferable tool for the mechanism-informed design and accelerated screening of high-performance BCC alloys for critical structural applications.
